content.text: The text reviews cholera morbus, summer diarrhoea/cholera infantum, pseudo-membranous enteritis, dysentery, typhlitis, intestinal ulcers, hemorrhage, and obstruction. It describes their symptoms, pathology, causes, diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, and largely historical treatments. Cholera morbus causes abrupt vomiting, watery diarrhoea, cramps, dehydration, collapse, and usually rapid recovery. Infantile summer diarrhoea is linked to heat, foul air, overcrowding, and improper or fermented feeding, especially bottle-feeding; cholera infantum is its severe, rapidly fatal form. Dysentery chiefly inflames and ulcerates the colon, producing tenesmus, mucus, pus, blood, and possible hepatic abscess. Typhlitis centers on the caecum or appendix and may cause abscess, perforation, or peritonitis. Intestinal ulcers may cause pain, diarrhoea, hemorrhage, or perforation. Management historically emphasized rest, diet, hygiene, irrigation, opiates, bismuth, ipecacuanha, stimulants, and surgery when obstruction or abscess occurred. A dysentery hospital once marched from July 26 to August 3, 1812, and patients improved rapidly after sheltering in a sheep-shed with fresh air and hay.
